On the 2nd August 2006 “The Herald” published the following news:

“MORE than 20 previously unseen paintings by Margaret Macdonald, the wife of Charles Rennie Mackintosh, and her artist sister Frances, have been discovered in the US. 
The watercolours, a series of paintings for a book of Arthurian legends, will be shown as part of the Glasgow Mackintosh festival this summer. 
The discovery of the paintings, thought to be a private commission which has ended up in the State University of New York, was yesterday described as "thrilling" by Pamela Robertson, curator of Glasgow University's Mackintosh collection. 
The paintings were found sewn into the pages of an edition of The Defence of Guenevere and Other Poems by William Morris, which had lain unnoticed in the university library at Buffalo for decades. 
They were discovered last year when John Edens, assistant director of libraries, came across the work while preparing for an exhibition of highlights from the collection.”

The paintings, apparently created in 1897, were bound into a copy of the 1902 Kelmscott Press edition of William Morris poetry book “The defence of Guenevere and other poems”, making it a one-of-a-kind volumen.

Some of the materials examined by Pamela Robertson indicate that the paintings constituted a specific commission, posibly by Thomas Glen Arthur, a noted Glasgow patrón of the arts, deceased in 1907.

***

El 2 de agosto de 2006, el periódico «The Herald» publicó la siguiente noticia:

«Más de 20 pinturas inéditas de Margaret Macdonald, esposa de Charles Rennie Mackintosh, y su hermana, la artista Frances, han sido descubiertas en Estados Unidos.
Las acuarelas, una serie de pinturas para un libro sobre leyendas artúricas, se exhibirán este verano como parte del Festival Mackintosh de Glasgow.
El descubrimiento de las pinturas, que se cree que fueron un encargo privado y que acabó en la Universidad Estatal de Nueva York, fue calificado ayer de «emocionante» por Pamela Robertson, conservadora de la colección Mackintosh de la Universidad de Glasgow.
Las pinturas fueron encontradas cosidas entre las páginas de una edición de La defensa de Ginebra y otros poemas de William Morris, que había permanecido olvidada durante décadas en la biblioteca universitaria de Buffalo.
Fueron descubiertas el año pasado cuando John Edens, subdirector de bibliotecas, las encontró mientras preparaba una exposición con las obras más destacadas de la colección.»

Las pinturas, aparentemente creadas en 1897, estaban encuadernadas en un ejemplar de la edición de 1902 de Kelmscott Press

recentItems.title: Happy Birthday Mr. Shakespeare !
recentItems.description:
Happy Birthday Mr. Shakespeare! 🌷

Music: Scarborough Fair by John Renbourn

William Shekespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon, where he was baptised on 26 April 1564. His date of birth is unknown but is traditionally observed on 23 April, Saint George's Day. This date, which can be traced to William Oldys and George Steevens, has proved appealing to biographers because Shakespeare died on the same date in 1616.

Anyway, we don’t find very appropriate to wish someone happy birthday on the day of his death. So, as the Folger Shakespeare Library decided to celebrate Shakespeare’s birthday on the 19th of April, we chosed to celebrate it today, with the same scientific basis, as the only preserved reference about dates is the date of baptism, the 26th of april.

Happy birthday, Mr. Shakespeare, whatever the day may be.!

recentItems.description:
Carmilla - Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu
Ilustraciones: Antonio Lorente
(Este es un canal sin ánimo de lucro, con el único objeto de compartir arte. Si aún así, los propietarios de las imágenes  entienden que estoy infringiendo sus derechos, ruego me lo comuniquen y quitaré el video.)

Música: Harry Robinson: suite from Countess Dracula (1971)

Carmilla is a Gothic novella in which a young woman named Laura details her relationship with a vampire in the form of a young woman named Carmilla. The first event that Laura details in the novella is an episode from her childhood: a six-year-old Laura is attempting to sleep when she is visited by a mysterious young lady (later revealed to be the vampire Carmilla, or at least a representation of Carmilla) who bites her on her breast. The narration then jumps forward thirteen years. Laura’s father receives a letter from his friend, General Spielsdorf, wherein the General reveals that his ward Bertha has died. The General implies that a monster of some sort has killed Bertha.

Later that day, a carriage carrying Carmilla and her mother crashes near Laura’s castle and the mother convinces Laura’s father to look after Carmilla for a few months while she attends to important business. Laura is excited to have Carmilla as a visitor, and the two of them are soon infatuated with each other. Soon after Carmilla’s arrival at the castle, local peasant girls are found dead, and a rumor starts that there is a vampire prowling the area. Laura and Carmilla spend most of their time together, and their intimacy grows. One night, Laura dreams that a large black cat pounces on her in her sleep and bites her breast. Laura then develops a strange, languorous illness that lasts months. Laura wakes one night from a terrible nightmare to find Carmilla at her bedside, but Carmilla escapes the room. Laura finds Carmilla’s room locked up, but Carmilla is not inside it. Laura’s father decides that Carmilla has sleepwalked and somehow found a way outside of her locked room. A doctor is sent for and is very concerned for Laura’s health. Laura’s father takes her on a trip to the village of Karnstein, in search of a priest. On the way, they meet the General, who tells them the story of Bertha’s death. Bertha’s story is exactly like Laura’s: she was infatuated with a young woman who was a guest and began to have disturbing dreams. The General is on a mission to revenge her death, and to that end he recruits Baron Vordenburg, an expert on vampires, to help him. The Baron discovers the location of Carmilla’s tomb and the vampire Carmilla is destroyed. The novella ends with Laura reminiscing about Carmilla, and saying that she sometimes fancies that she hears Carmilla’s footsteps at her door.

Some say that  “Pre-dating Dracula by twenty-six years, Carmilla is the original vampire story” but “Carmilla” was first serialised in the literary magazine The Dark Blue in late 1871 and early 1872, while John William Polidori (Lord Byron’s doctor and Dante Gabriel Rossetti ‘s uncle) published his novel “The vampyre” in 1819, “pre-dating Carmilla” by 53 years.

Antonio Lorente (26 de julio de 1987) es un ilustrador español.
En 2005-2010 se licencia en Bellas Artes en la Universidad Politécnica de Valencia. Fijando su residencia en Portugal y Reino Unido, donde continuó desarrollando su carrera y estilo.
Se especializó en animación 2D y decidió abandonarlo para trabajar con imagen fija, creador de personajes y fondista. En 2012 realizó su primera muestra individual en la casa del cine de su ciudad natal6 y en los años siguientes su trabajo, junto al de otros ilustradores, se expuso en la Biblioteca Nacional de España y por galerías de Reino Unido, Estados Unidos e Italia.
Algunos de sus álbumes ilustrados los ha realizado junto a su hermana y escritora María Jesús Lorente: La princesa Aburrida en 2016, Yago (2017), Genios "El eco fantasma de sus voces" (2018), libro becado por EmprendeDiseño de Factoría Cultural en Matadero, Madrid.

Dante Alighieri was born in Florence, Italy. The date of his birth is believed to be around 1265.

“Il di primo di maggio dell’anno 1274 Dante Allighieri, giovinetto di nove anni compiuti, vide la prima volta Beatrice giovinetta d’anni otto e quattro mesi; e cominciò allora ad amarla.”
(La Vita Di Beatrice Portinari – Giovanni Federzoni – Bologna 1905)

Dante said he first met Beatrice Portinari, daughter of Folco Portinari, when he was nine (she was eight and some months), and he claimed to have fallen in love with her "at first sight"

Dante claimed to have seen Beatrice again frequently after he turned 18, exchanging greetings with her in the streets of Florence, although painters and poets refer  to only four encounters in Florence, and the Divine Comedy records one more in paradise.

1st encounter 1st may 1274, when Dante was 9 years old.

2nd encounter  1st may 1283, when Dante was 18 years old, he meets Beatrice – already married -  “vestita di colore bianchissimo, in mezzo di due gentili donne” (dressed in the most white color, in the midle of two gente ladies)  and she greeted him.

3rd encounter, in some street of Florence, Beatrice refuses to greet Dante, likely as a reaction against Dante’s publicly known relation with a florentine young girl  .

4th encounter, at a wedding, and she refuses anew to greet him.

5th encounter at Paradise.

José Segrelles Albert (18 March 1885 - 3 March 1969) was a Spanish painter, illustrator and poster desginer. He was the uncle of cartoonists and painters Eustaquio and Vicente Segrelles.
Segrelles was born in Albaida, Valencia province, in 1885. He studied in the Saint Charles Royal Academy of Fine Arts of Valencia and at Escola de la Llotja in Barcelona. 
He dedicated his entire life to illustrating literary works, mainly working for Editorial Araluce’s Universal Literature adapted for children. He also published in english and american magazines, such as The Illustrated London News (he was a regular contributor in the Christmas specials between 1927 and 1934), The American Weekly, Redbook, Cosmopolitan . . .
Although the main amount of his works as an illustrator were watercolours,  from 1940 he received a great number of orders for oil paintings to be exhibited in churches.
He died in his hometown of Albaida in 1969.
NOTE: Although all the illustrations are by José Segrelles, the frames of the Tales titles are by Georges Rochegrosse and Errol Le Cain
....
Josep Segrelles Albert (Albaida; 18 de marzo de 1885 - Albaida, 3 de marzo de 1969) fue un pintor, cartelista e ilustrador español. Es tío de los historietistas y pintores Eustaquio Segrelles y Vicente Segrelles.
Segrelles nació en Albaida, provincia de Valencia, en 1885. Estudió en la Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Carlos, en Valencia,  y en la Escola de la Llotja en Barcelona. 
Se dedicó toda su vida a la ilustración de obras literarias, especialmente a raíz de La Literatura Universal adaptada para los niños editada por Araluce. También colaboró como ilustrador en revistas inglesas (en los especiales de Navidad de  The Illustrated London News entre 1927 y 1934), The American Weecly, Redbook, Cosmopolitan . . .
Aunque la parte principal de su obra como ilustrador seguía la técnica de la acuarela, a partir de 1940 recibió gran cantidad de encargos para pinturas al óleo en iglesias.
Murió en su ciudad natal de Albaida en 1969.
NOTA: Aunque todas las ilustraciones son de José Segrelles, los marcos de los títulos de los cuentos son de Georges Rochegrosse y de Errol Le Cain.

The months of this video (illustrations from Marthe Romme) are the months of the French Republican Calendar, used by the French republican governements from late 1793 to 1805 . Although the French Republican Calendar placed the beginning of the year at the day of the autumnal equinox, in our video we have placed the beginning at the day of the winter solstice, in order to  present the year as close as posible to our usual year.

Since the dates of the zodiac almost coincide with those of the french republican calendar, we have added after each month the corresponding zodiac sign (illustrations from Raymond Peynet)

Finally, the illustrations of the seasons are from Paul Allier.

recentItems.description:
Henry James’ Turn of the Screw 👻👻👻 
Ilustraciones: Ana Juan 2013
Música: “Turn of the Screw” film 1992
Jane Burden Morris’  Channel:
http://www.youtube.com/user/Laika231

Ana Juan ilustra “Otra vuelta de tuerca” de Henry James, un clásico del terror gótico reinterpretado a través de su estilo perturbador e inconfundible.
Ana Juan crea una atmósfera opresiva y gótica que se ajusta perfectamente al mundo onírico y subconsciente de sus ilustraciones y opta por un planteamiento conceptual y, también, gráfico dual que evite plegarse al texto de manera literal. Por un lado, aprovecha las entradas de los capítulos para sintetizar el misterio y el drama de los acontecimientos que precedieron a la llegada de la protagonista.
Para ello, se vale de unas ilustraciones de pequeño formato realizadas con tan solo dos colores, en las que establece una analogía entre los protagonistas de la novela y unos personajes alegóricos. De este modo, nos ofrece una posible visión de los hechos, que recrean el ambiente y producen una gran sensación de angustia e inquietud al lector.
Otra vuelta de tuerca está considerada la novela de fantasmas por antonomasia y un hito insoslayable en la historia de la literatura universal. Su temática resulta de lo más actual a pesar de haber sido escrita en el año 1898.

Ana Juan (Valencia, España) es ilustradora y escritora. Licenciada en Bellas Artes, empezó su trayectoria profesional a mediados de los ochenta en las revistas La Luna de Madrid y Madriz. En 1995 apareció su primera portada en The New Yorker, a la que seguirían muchas más. En 2001 publicó sus libros Amantes (1000editions) y Snowhite (Edicions de Ponent), pero desde 2002 se ha dedicado sobre todo a la ilustración para libros infantiles. Entre otros muchos reconocimientos, en 2010, el Ministerio de Cultura le concedió el Premio Nacional de Ilustración.

recentItems.description:
Music: “Rachmaninoff Piano Concerto No. 2 in C Minor Op. 18 - 2. Adagio sostenuto” Valentina Lisitsa 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SHN3Yexwu8A

BURNE JONES’ THE PERSEUS STORY
(1875 – unfinished)

In 1875 the politician Lord Arthur Balfour (Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1902 to 1905) commissioned Burne-Jones to create a series of paintings for the music room of his London home. Burne-Jones’s  work was often inspired by mythology and legend and presented an imaginative world focused on beauty of form and spirit. A re-telling of the Perseus myth in William Morris’s poem ‘The Earthly Paradise’ provided the subject.  Burne-Jones worked on the project for ten years but it was never completed. Southampton Art Gallery has ten full-size studies in gouache, ‘cartoons’ which Burne-Jones made to perfect his designs before beginning the final paintings in oil.

Perseus and the Graiae was to be the pivotal scene of Edward Burne-Jones’s Perseus Series. As such, several versions created between 1875-1892 exist in the form of four successive versions: a small study (1875-76), a full-size gouache cartoon (1877-80), a gilded low–relief oak panel (1877-88), and an oil painting (1892) created after the original oak panel was unfavourably received.

Both the gouache cartoon and the gilded low-relief oak panel include a text with the full story of the Perseus myth, which could be translated as follows:

“Pallas Athena spurred Perseus to action with her urging, and equipped him with arms. The Graiae revealed to him the remote home of the nymphs. From here he went with wings on his feet and with his head shrouded in darkness, and with his sword he struck the one mortal Gorgon, the others being immortal. Her two sisters arose and pursued him. Next he turned Atlas to stone. The sea serpent was slain and Andromeda rescued, and the comrades of Phineas became lumps of rock. Then Andromeda looked in a mirror with wonder at the dreadful Medusa.”

The original idea was to combine four low-relief panels as the above described and six oil paintings, but the public reaction at the showing of the “Perseus and the Graiae” panel at the Grosvenor Gallery discouraged the painter to continue with this scheme and decided to produce ten oil paintings.

He finished ten gouache panels, intended ad previous studies, but never completed more tan five oil panels of the whole series.
